As of 220 AM EDT Thursday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Current surface analysis this morning shows a weak 
shortwave continuing to push east across the region. Most radar 
returns are not making it to the ground as a result of a decent 
surface dry layer. That said, isentropic lift across the southern 
tier of New York is leading to some light shower activity that 
stretches back into the Great Lakes. As today progresses this 
boundary will lift north encountering a dry sfc-700mb level which 
will help reduce precipitation chances for the most part today. 
Clouds will be the main change as cloud cover increases throughout 
the day. A few isolated light showers and/or sprinkles in northern 
New York, and some upslope mist and mountain top clouds will be 
possible after noon today, but most locations today look to remain 
dry. The main weather impacts today will be wind driven. A 
tightening pressure gradient will allow for good southerly channeled 
flow in the Champlain Valley and St. Lawrence Valley this afternoon 
as a 40-50 knot LLJ in the 850-925mb layer builds across the region. 
Gusts 20-30 MPH are expected late this morning into this evening 
before more steadier rain arrives late tonight, stabilizing and 
weakening our gusts. While current lake winds are just below Lake 
Wind Advisory criteria (25 knots), a Lake Wind Advisory will likely 
be needed for this afternoon and evening, when winds are expected to 
increase. Southerly flow will also aid in advecting some warmer air 
into the region, as highs increase into the upper 60s to low 70s 
today.

Steadier rain will arrive overnight tonight as a cold front pushes 
into the region from west to east. Moisture associated with this 
front is reminiscent of a summer-like pattern, as this air mass 
originates from the tropical east Pacific. PWs will increase to 1.5-
1.8" in the wider valleys of the area; in the 99th percentile for 
this time of year. While PWs will be anomalously high, the 
stretching the system, in addition to its progressive nature, will 
help keep higher totals at bay. Ensembles continue to keep 
probabilities of exceeding 1" at 10% or lower. Hi res model 
guidance generally depicts a quarter to half an inch of rain for 
much of northern New York, and near the International Border, with a 
quarter or less in the western Champlain Valley and southern 
Vermont, due to some shadowing effects. The winners from this system 
will be across the northwestern upslope regions of the Adirondacks 
and northern Greens where around three quarters of an inch is 
expected. Given the high PWs, some downpours, and locally heavier 
rainfall amounts will be possible in the aforementioned locations. 

A secondary clearing cold front, depicted in the higher resolution 
models looks to pass through Friday afternoon. Some additional 
convergent flow and meager instability may allow for some additional 
showers across southern Vermont, though these look isolated to 
scattered at best. Dewpoints behind this second front will fall
from near 60 Friday afternoon, to the upper 30s to low 40s by 
Saturday afternoon. Drying top down Friday night into Saturday 
will clear the region of cloud cover with more sunny skies. 
Temperatures will also follow suit, cooling from the mid 60s on 
Friday to the upper 50s to near 60 by Saturday. More seasonable 
temperatures will continue into the latter portion of the 
weekend.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Closed low across Hudson-James Bay this weekend will 
rotate a few shortwaves that will impact our area late weekend into 
next week.

The first largely stays across Canada with an associated cold front 
from the primary surface low well north in Canada moving across the 
northern Great Lakes then northern NY-New England Sunday night but 
immediately on its heels a larger, stronger and more amplified 
shortwave drops SSE into the region on Monday with much colder air 
and breezy conditions.

The initial front may bring a shower/two across the northern border 
but then the front waits for the more robust system during Monday 
with increased instability due to strong cold air advection aloft 
for better chance of showers, especially terrain driven.

Continued cold air advection and cyclonic NW flow Monday night will 
keep some clouds and gradient so not the coldest night. 

Upper level shortwave ridging and surface high building into the 
region Tue-Tue ngt will bring the coldest air of this young season 
with frost-freeze likely everywhere except immediately along Lake 
Champlain. Tuesday morning lows will be in the 20s-30s with highs in 
the 50s with some upper 40s as well.

Ridging at all levels exits Wednesday with return flow and 
moderating temperatures and a chance of showers Wed ngt.
